metadata.title: The Relationships Among ICT-Related Psychological Factors, School Contextual Factors and Secondary Students’ Reading Performance: A Multilevel Analysis Across 47 Economies

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 47 economies, selecting only economies that administered the ICT Familiarity Questionnaire and excluding specific countries due to implausible response behavior or missing student- or school-level questionnaire information. The analysis is conducted with three-level hierarchical linear modeling (students nested within schools nested within countries) in R (lme4), but the manuscript does not report the use of PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight procedure. Because the paper does not mention weight variables (e.g., student design weights) or complex survey variance estimation, it is unclear whether population-representative weighting was applied. The reported preprocessing focuses on country exclusions and constructing composite ICT psychological indexes and school contextual factors; no PV handling or survey-weighted estimation details are provided.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is the PISA 2018 computer-based reading score (READ) analyzed via multilevel linear modeling, but the paper does not describe whether READ is treated as a PV-based achievement score or as an IRT/WLE-type scale score. Because the manuscript also does not report a missing-data strategy for student- or school-level variables beyond excluding certain economies with large proportions of missing factors, the missing-data handling for the remaining analytic sample is not fully documented. This is a reporting gap: PISA datasets typically require explicit handling of missing questionnaire responses and (for achievement) PVs, yet the paper provides limited methodological detail on these points.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PISA 2018 computer-based reading assessment and the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire. Only economies that completed the ICT Familiarity Questionnaire were selected. Spain was excluded due to implausible response behavior; Austria was excluded because large proportions of student-level factors were missing; New Zealand and Sweden were excluded because large proportions of school-level factors were missing; Chinese Taipei was excluded because economic background information was missing. The final analytic sample comprises 222,293 secondary students from 10,103 schools representing 47 economies.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (computer-based reading literacy), secondary students (15-year-olds)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Three-level HLM (students within schools within countries). Student-level effects: ICT interest b=6.7771 (SE=0.1950, p<.001); ICT autonomy b=10.2882 (SE=0.2266, p<.001); ICT competence b=3.8641 (SE=0.2321, p<.001); ICT social interaction b=-12.8349 (SE=0.2075, p<.001). Cross-level interactions: SCHICTD×AUTICT b=0.5113 (SE=0.2069, p=.0135); SCHICTD×SOIAICT b=-1.3154 (SE=0.2083, p<.001). Simple slopes at SCHICTD: AUTICT b=9.7485 (high) vs b=8.7064 (low); SOIAICT b=-4.4478 (high) vs b=-1.2794 (low).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged ICT interest, ICT autonomy, ICT competence, and ICT social interaction (with school ICT device support as a cross-level moderator) to predict reading performance, finding that ICT interest/autonomy/competence were positively associated with reading performance while ICT social interaction was negatively associated. It also found that greater school support in ICT devices accentuated the positive autonomy–reading relationship and strengthened the negative social-interaction–reading relationship. This indicates that strengthening students’ ICT-related autonomy and competence—while carefully managing socially oriented ICT use in device-rich schools—may improve digital-age reading outcomes, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PISA 2018 computer-based reading literacy performance (READ) for 222,293 secondary students nested within 10,103 schools across 47 economies, using the optional ICT Familiarity Questionnaire plus student and school questionnaires. The authors fit three-level hierarchical linear models (students within schools within countries) and report statistically significant associations consistent with Self-Determination Theory: ICT interest, autonomy, and competence are positively related to reading performance, whereas perceived social interaction in ICT use is negatively related. Cross-level moderation shows that quantity-oriented school support in ICT devices accentuates both the autonomy benefit and the social-interaction disadvantage, while quality-oriented support via teachers’ capacity to integrate technology strengthens the competence benefit and buffers the social-interaction disadvantage. Model fit is evaluated using deviance, AIC/BIC, and effect sizes (f2), but the paper does not report PV handling or a detailed missing-data strategy beyond country exclusions, and causality cannot be inferred due to the cross-sectional design.
